title: SQL Formatter
description: SQL Formatter helps people format SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax and review the result before using it in another system.
intro: SQL Formatter is for a concrete handoff: take SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax from a real task, produce the form the next editor, API, document, or workflow expects, and keep enough context to verify what changed.
audience: Application developers, data analysts, database reviewers, and support engineers
input: A representative sample of SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax copied from the API, file, codebase, log, document, or request involved in the task.
outcome: A sql formatter result that preserves the intended meaning and is ready to test in its destination.
review: Check SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax, malformed input, escaped values, and destination-specific rules before relying on the result.
bestFor: Small and medium SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax samples used for debugging, documentation, migration preparation, review, and reproducible tests.
steps: Paste a representative SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax from the task you are working on.
Run SQL Formatter and compare the first meaningful change with the source.
Inspect SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax plus any destination-specific constraints.
Copy or download the result, then validate it in the editor, runtime, API, form, or publishing system where it will be used.
useCases: SQL Formatter for a real development or integration task rather than a synthetic keyword example.
Preparing SQL Formatter input and output for a bug report, documentation page, test fixture, or technical handoff.
Using SQL Formatter to compare the source and result before a migration, import, release, or review.
SQL Formatter helps catch structural or meaning-changing mistakes before the output reaches another system.

examples.title: SQL Formatter with a representative sample
examples.description: This SQL Formatter example uses SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax that resembles a small production fixture, so the main change can be checked line by line.
examples.input: select customer_id,count(*) as orders from purchases where created_at>=current_date-30 group by customer_id having count(*)>2;
examples.output:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM purchases
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

examples.title: SQL Formatter edge-case review
examples.description: The second SQL Formatter pass focuses on the part most likely to fail: nested values, escaping, or destination rules.
examples.input:
select customer_id,count(*) as orders from purchases where created_at>=current_date-30 group by customer_id having count(*)>2;

Review case: preserve empty, repeated, or non-ASCII values where applicable.
examples.output:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM purchases
WHERE created_at >= CURRENT_DATE - 30
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;

Review note: confirm this result in the destination workflow.

tips: Keep the original SQL Formatter input beside the result until the destination check passes.
Use realistic SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax instead of a one-word sample when validating SQL Formatter.
Do not assume the visual cleanup from SQL Formatter proves that SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax is valid.
Run the normal project, API, schema, browser, or editorial validation after using SQL Formatter.

faq.question: Who uses SQL Formatter?
faq.answer: Application developers, data analysts, database reviewers, and support engineers use SQL Formatter when they need to format SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax before continuing work in another editor, system, or document.

faq.question: What should I paste into SQL Formatter?
faq.answer: Paste a focused but representative sample of SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax into SQL Formatter. Include the nesting, punctuation, characters, or edge cases that affect the real task.

faq.question: What does SQL Formatter change?
faq.answer: SQL Formatter changes the representation needed for this task. Compare the output with the source to confirm that values and intended meaning remain correct.

faq.question: What should I check after using SQL Formatter?
faq.answer: After SQL Formatter, review SQL clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax, escaped values, malformed input, and the rules enforced by the destination system.

faq.question: Can I use the SQL Formatter output in production?
faq.answer: Use the SQL Formatter result as reviewed working output, then run the destination system's normal validation, tests, schema checks, or editorial review before production use.

faq.question: Does SQL Formatter store my input?
faq.answer: SQL Formatter has no account or saved-history feature. Even so, remove passwords, private keys, session cookies, personal data, and production secrets before using any online tool.

keywords: format sql clauses, joins, expressions, and dialect-specific syntax
commonMistakes: Running SQL Formatter with a sample that does not represent the real input.
Using the SQL Formatter result without comparing it with the original source.
Skipping validation in the editor, runtime, API, or document that receives the output.
